features.name: Great Dark Spot
features.description: The Great Dark Spot was a giant anticyclonic storm photographed by Voyager 2 in 1989, comparable in size to Earth. Unlike Jupiter's Great Red Spot, Neptune's dark spots appear and vanish over timescales of just a few years, showing that the planet's atmosphere is much more transient and mobile.

details.label: Observed
details.value: Voyager 2, 1989

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: By the time Hubble looked again in 1994, the original Great Dark Spot had already disappeared.

features.name: Dark Spot Jr.
features.description: After Voyager's Great Dark Spot vanished, Hubble discovered a new generation of dark storms forming at different latitudes. These shifting systems show that Neptune's atmosphere can reorganize rapidly, with vortices migrating and dissipating on surprisingly short timescales.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune's dark vortices have been seen drifting toward the equator, where some appear to break apart and disappear.

features.name: The Scooter
features.description: The Scooter is a bright, fast-moving methane-ice cloud system that raced around Neptune much faster than the Great Dark Spot during the Voyager 2 flyby. It revealed the extreme wind shear in Neptune's atmosphere, where some cloud systems outrun others embedded deeper below.

details.label: Wind context
details.value: Linked to some of the fastest measured winds in the Solar System

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Voyager images showed the Scooter lapping the planet faster than the larger dark storm beside it.

features.name: South Polar Vortex
features.description: Neptune's south pole hosts a warm polar vortex with a compact eye-like structure surrounded by bright methane clouds. Infrared observations show warmer air descending there, making it one of the most distinctive polar weather systems in the outer Solar System.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The south polar vortex has often been compared to a giant hurricane, even though Neptune has no solid surface beneath it.

features.name: Equatorial Methane Haze
features.description: Neptune's equatorial region is wrapped in a bright methane-ice haze where sunlight scatters off high-altitude clouds. This pale band helps distinguish vertical structure in an atmosphere otherwise dominated by deep blue methane absorption.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune's blue colour comes largely from methane absorbing red light, leaving the shorter blue wavelengths to dominate.

features.name: Mid-Latitude Bands
features.description: Subtle bright and dark bands wrap Neptune's mid-latitudes, tracing powerful east-west jet streams. They are fainter than Jupiter's belts but still reveal a deeply organized atmosphere beneath the planet's calmer telescopic appearance.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some of Neptune's jet streams reach supersonic speeds relative to the planet's internal sound speed estimates.

features.name: North Polar Region
features.description: The north polar region appears less dramatically structured than the south in many observations, but it still shows seasonal haze, polar circulation, and changes tied to Neptune's long year. Because each season lasts decades, the poles evolve slowly from our perspective.

details.label: Year length
details.value: About 165 Earth years

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: A single Neptunian season lasts more than 40 Earth years.

features.name: South Polar Region
features.description: Neptune's south polar region is marked by bright methane clouds and a warm central vortex, making it the most visually distinctive pole on the planet. It became a major target for infrared telescopes trying to understand how Neptune transports heat from its interior.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Neptune radiates more than twice as much energy as it receives from the Sun, helping power its active weather.

features.name: Triton and the Neptune System
features.description: Neptune's broader system is dominated by Triton, a captured Kuiper Belt object that orbits backward relative to Neptune's rotation. That unusual moon, along with Neptune's faint rings and remote location, makes the planet feel more like the threshold of the Kuiper Belt than just another giant planet.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Triton's retrograde orbit strongly suggests it was captured rather than formed alongside Neptune.

features.name: Galle Ring
features.description: The Galle ring is the innermost of Neptune's rings, appearing as a broad but extremely faint band of dark reddish material. Named for Johann Galle, who first observed Neptune mathematically before it was seen visually.

details.label: Distance
details.value: 40,900 – 42,900 km from center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Galle ring is so faint it was one of the last Uranian rings to be confirmed by Voyager 2.

features.name: Le Verrier Ring
features.description: The Le Verrier ring is a narrow, relatively bright ring named for Urbain Le Verrier, whose mathematical predictions led to Neptune's discovery. It is one of the more conspicuous components of Neptune's faint ring system.

details.label: Distance
details.value: ~53,200 km from center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Le Verrier and Galle corresponded about Neptune's position before it was observed, making this ring's namesake part of a famous astronomical rivalry.

features.name: Lassell Ring
features.description: The Lassell ring is an extremely faint, broad sheet of material extending outward from the Le Verrier ring. Named for William Lassell, who discovered Triton just weeks after Neptune itself was found.

details.label: Distance
details.value: 53,200 – 57,200 km from center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Lassell ring is so faint and diffuse it may be largely sustained by dust from meteoroid impacts on smaller moons.

features.name: Adams Ring
features.description: The Adams ring is Neptune's most famous ring, known for containing the remarkable 'ring arcs' — clumps of material named Fraternité, Égalité, Liberté, and Courage that orbit together. These arcs are held in place by the moon Galatea through gravitational interactions.

details.label: Distance
details.value: ~63,932 km from center

details.label: Arcs
details.value: Fraternité, Égalité, Liberté, Courage

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The Adams ring arcs are unique in the Solar System — nowhere else do ring particles clump so dramatically into stable, named segments.

features.name: Naiad
features.description: Naiad is Neptune's innermost known moon, a small dark body discovered in Voyager 2 images in 1989. It circles so close to Neptune that one orbit takes only about seven hours, and its path is locked in a remarkable dance with nearby Thalassa that keeps the two tiny moons from close encounters.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 48,200 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 2.56 units from Neptune's centre, outside the Galle ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 66 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Naiad and Thalassa avoid each other through a repeating orbital pattern sometimes described as a tiny cosmic dance.

features.name: Thalassa
features.description: Thalassa is one of Neptune's innermost small moons, orbiting just beyond Naiad in the dense inner system found by Voyager 2. It is irregular, dark, and probably built from icy rubble, and its resonant relationship with Naiad is one of the most elegant orbital patterns known around Neptune.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 50,100 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 2.66 units from Neptune's centre, outside the Galle ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 82 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Thalassa repeatedly passes over and under Naiad's tilted path instead of meeting it head-on.

features.name: Despina
features.description: Despina is a small inner moon orbiting close to Neptune's faint ring system. Its gravity is linked to the narrow Le Verrier ring, making it part of the machinery that keeps Neptune's dim rings structured instead of fading into a smooth dusty sheet.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 52,500 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 2.84 units from Neptune's centre, just inside the Le Verrier ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 150 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Despina orbits in the same compact region as Neptune's main rings, helping turn the moon system and ring system into one connected structure.

features.name: Galatea
features.description: Galatea is a small inner moon best known for its relationship with Neptune's Adams ring. Its gravity helps confine the famous ring arcs, where dusty material bunches into named clumps instead of spreading evenly around the planet.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 62,000 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 3.42 units from Neptune's centre, just inside the Adams ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 176 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Galatea is the moon that helps make Neptune's Adams ring arcs one of the strangest ring features in the Solar System.

features.name: Larissa
features.description: Larissa is an irregular inner moon that was first noticed from Earth in 1981 when it briefly blocked a background star, then confirmed by Voyager 2 in 1989. It orbits beyond Galatea and is large enough to be a distinct lumpy world, but still far too small for gravity to pull it round.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 73,500 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 3.82 units from Neptune's centre, outside the Adams ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 194 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Larissa was suspected before Voyager arrived because it made a star blink out during an occultation.

features.name: Proteus
features.description: Proteus is the largest of Neptune's inner moons and one of the darkest objects Voyager 2 photographed there. At roughly 420 kilometres across, it is close to the size where gravity could start pulling a body into a rounded shape, yet Proteus remains heavily cratered and irregular.

details.label: Real orbit
details.value: About 117,600 km from Neptune's centre

details.label: Scene orbit
details.value: 4.75 units from Neptune's centre, outside the Adams ring

details.label: Approximate diameter
details.value: About 420 km

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Proteus is about as large as an icy moon can get before self-gravity starts making it much rounder.
